# certstream-server-rust

> A Certificate Transparency log streaming server written in Rust. It monitors Chrome- and Apple-trusted CT logs and streams newly issued TLS certificates over WebSocket and SSE. It supports both RFC 6962 and static-ct-api logs in one binary and is compatible with clients written for certstream-server and certstream-server-go.

Typical uses include phishing and typosquat detection, brand monitoring, attack surface discovery, threat intelligence pipelines, certificate inventory, and research on newly issued certificates.

On one measured deployment, the server processed around 420 certificates and 700 domain names per second, or roughly 36 million certificates and 62 million domain names per day, while using about 80 MB RSS and 0.2 CPU cores.

## Docs

- [Home](https://certstream.dev/): project overview, installation options, and features
- [API documentation](https://certstream.dev/docs.html): WebSocket and SSE endpoints, message formats, environment variables, and REST API
- [Quick start](https://certstream.dev/quickstart.html): running the server and connecting a client
- [Architecture](https://certstream.dev/architecture.html): ingest pipeline, broadcast path, deduplication, and state persistence

## Engineering writing

- [Why jemalloc RSS is 4x the live heap](https://certstream.dev/blog/jemalloc-transparent-huge-pages-rss.html): investigating 358 MB process RSS with 52 MB reported as allocated by jemalloc, and how Transparent Huge Pages accounted for most of the gap on the affected host
- [Reading Certificate Transparency tiles without a checkpoint](https://certstream.dev/blog/ct-logs-tiles-without-checkpoint.html): reading static-ct-api tiles from logs that return 404 for `/checkpoint`, using the tree size from `get-sth`, and handling the edge cases that appeared in production
- [HTTP/2 multiplexing vs per-connection rate limits](https://certstream.dev/blog/http2-multiplexing-vs-per-connection-rate-limits.html): testing whether forcing HTTP/1.1 improves catch-up throughput, measuring the connection count, and finding that the main limit was the number of entries returned per request
